source:
Let's create a single-player version of "Laser Grid Survival" where the user plays against AI bots.

Game Setup:
When the game starts, automatically spawn 30 AI-controlled humanoid bots into the lobby alongside the main player. Give the bots basic pathfinding scripts so they run forward toward the objective during the safe phases, but make them occasionally make mistakes and fail so the player has competition.

Game 1: Motion Sensor Rush
Build a long metallic hallway with a pulsing laser core computer at the end. Every few seconds, a glowing grid line sweeps the hallway.
- When the line is BLUE, the player and the AI bots sprint forward.
- When the line turns RED, an alarm blares. The player and the AI bots must freeze. Write a script for the AI bots so that 15% of them randomly fail to stop moving in time. Any player or bot that moves during the RED phase gets zapped by a laser and eliminated.

Game 2: Gravity Fractures
A high-tech chasm crossed by pairs of neon steps (one solid, one a fake holographic illusion). Write a script for the remaining AI bots so they take turns guessing which step to step on. If a bot guesses wrong, it falls and is eliminated, clearing the path or showing the player which way is safe.

Visual Style:
A gritty, sci-fi cyber-bunker. The player and bots wear simple metallic suits. Hostile NPCs are hovering security drones.

image_prompt.text: The lobby where the player and the thirty bots gather before and between the two games, sized for the full field without bottlenecking at the exits
A prominent wall in the lobby sized to host the surviving-player count and results board
Somewhere out of play for eliminated bots and the player to wait and watch the rest of the round
The markers that move everyone from the lobby into Motion Sensor Rush and then into Gravity Fractures
a long narrow metallic hallway with industrial wall and floor panels forming the run of Motion Sensor Rush
a pulsing laser core computer at the far end of the hallway as the thing being run toward
a glowing grid line that sweeps the length of the hallway, blue during the sprint phase and red during the freeze phase
a high-tech chasm crossed by pairs of neon steps, one of each pair solid and one a holographic illusion that drops you
hovering security drones patrolling as hostile NPCs

layout_placement.text: The leaderboard surface itself, tracking who is still alive across both games
Detection regions registering a successful crossing, a freeze violation, and a fall from the chasm
Lobby-to-stage transport into each of the two games and back at round end
laser elimination volumes along the hallway that fire on anything moving while the sweep line is red
spawn points in the lobby for the player and thirty AI bots

notes: Two separate staged games plus a lobby, so the shape is the isolated stage and the route carries P4.
The paired real-and-fake neon steps are exactly the obstacle-guess concept, but Obby and Platformer was not loaded for this prompt, so it is carried as free text rather than promoted to that ID.
Nothing in Party and Casual expresses NPC opponents. Thirty scripted bots, their pathfinding, and the fifteen percent failure rate all sit outside the handoff.

open_questions.ask: How long should the hallway be - a sprint of a few seconds, or a run that takes most of a minute?
What ends the experience - surviving both games, or being the last one standing against the bots?

coverage_missing.ask: How long is the hallway and how wide is the chasm crossing?
Does the run end after the second game, or loop?
Do the two games share one bunker interior, or are they genuinely separate places?

answers.ask: How long should the hallway be - a sprint of a few seconds, or a run that takes most of a minute?
answers.answer: Make it a short hallway run that takes roughly 20–30 seconds when the player handles the blue/red phases correctly; keep the first game compact and replayable.

answers.ask: What ends the experience - surviving both games, or being the last one standing against the bots?
answers.answer: The experience ends when the player survives both games and reaches the end of Gravity Fractures; the bots provide competition and can be eliminated, but last-one-standing is not required.
